title: Strings and UTF-8
summary: Create and grow Strings, join them with + and format!, understand why s[0] does not compile, and work with text as bytes, chars or slices safely.

sections: TRPL 8.2 Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings
TRPL 8.2 Methods for Iterating Over Strings

blocks.md:
Strings trip up newcomers to Rust more than almost anything else, for three reasons: Rust makes possible errors visible, strings are more complicated than they look, and text is stored as **UTF-8**. This lesson goes through each.

Rust has one string type in the core language, the string slice `&str` (chapter 4). The standard library adds **`String`**: an owned, growable, UTF-8 encoded text buffer. Under the hood, a `String` is a wrapper around a `Vec<u8>` that guarantees the bytes are always valid UTF-8.

blocks.output: foo! | initial contents | initial contents | Dobrý den

blocks.title: Joining strings
blocks.md:
`+` joins two strings, with a twist: it **takes ownership of the left side** and borrows the right side. Its signature is roughly `fn add(self, s: &str) -> String`. It reuses the left String's buffer and appends a copy of the right, which is efficient but means the left String is moved.

For anything more complicated, use `format!`, which works like `println!` but returns a `String` and takes no ownership:

blocks.output:
Hello, world! (world! still usable)
tic-tac-toe; tic tac toe are all still usable
blocks.explain: `&s2` is a `&String`, but `+` wants a `&str`. The compiler converts it automatically (deref coercion).

blocks.title: Why s[0] does not compile
blocks.md: In many languages `s[0]` gives the first character. In Rust it is a compile error: `` the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}` ``. To see why, look at how UTF-8 stores text. Each character takes **1 to 4 bytes**: ASCII letters take 1, most accented Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic letters take 2, most Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters take 3, and emoji take 4.

blocks.output:
12 chars, 24 bytes
first two bytes: [208, 151]
first char: Some('З')
blocks.explain: `len()` is the length in **bytes**. The first letter, `З`, is two bytes, 208 and 151. If `hello[0]` returned a byte, it would return 208, which is not a character at all. Rather than return something surprising, Rust does not let you index a string by position. A second reason: indexing is expected to be instant, but finding the n-th character requires scanning from the start.

blocks.title: Three ways to look at text
blocks.md:
Ask yourself which you mean:
- **bytes**: `s.bytes()` or `s.as_bytes()`, the raw UTF-8 (`u8` values). Right for network protocols and file formats.
- **chars**: `s.chars()`, Unicode scalar values. Right for most text processing.
- **grapheme clusters**: what a person calls a "letter". The Hindi word नमस्ते is 18 bytes, 6 chars, but 4 graphemes. The standard library does not provide these; the `unicode-segmentation` crate does.

blocks.title: Slicing needs care
blocks.md: Byte-range slices work (`&s[0..4]`), but a range that cuts a character in half **panics** at run time: `&s[0..1]` on `"Здравствуйте"` fails with `byte index 1 is not a char boundary`. To slice by characters, find the byte position first, for example with `s.char_indices()`, which gives each character together with its byte offset.

blocks.title: Initials and reversing
blocks.md: Write `initials` (the first character of each word, uppercase, joined with dots: `"ada lovelace"` → `"A.L."`) and `reverse` (the characters in reverse order, which must work for non-ASCII text). Use `chars()`, never byte indexes.
hints: `for word in name.split_whitespace()` and `word.chars().next()` gives the first char as an `Option<char>`.
`c.to_uppercase()` returns an iterator (some characters uppercase to several); `.to_string()` turns it into a String you can `push_str`.
`reverse`: `s.chars().rev().collect()` builds a String from the reversed chars.

blocks.title: Text utilities
blocks.goal: Process text correctly whatever language it is in.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn char_count(s: &str) -> usize`: the number of chars (not bytes).
- `pub fn pig_latin(word: &str) -> String`: from *The Rust Programming Language*'s exercise list. A word starting with a vowel gets `-hay` added (`apple` → `apple-hay`); otherwise the first char moves to the end with `ay` (`first` → `irst-fay`). Lowercase ASCII input.
- `pub fn truncate_chars(s: &str, max: usize) -> String`: at most `max` chars; if anything was cut, end with `…` (which counts toward `max`). `max` is at least 1.
- `pub fn word_count(s: &str) -> usize`: words separated by any whitespace.
hints: `pig_latin`: `let mut chars = word.chars(); let first = chars.next()`; the rest is `chars.as_str()`.
`truncate_chars`: if `char_count(s) <= max` return `s.to_string()`; else take `max - 1` chars with `s.chars().take(max - 1).collect::<String>()` and push `'…'`.
blocks.solution_explain: Everything goes through `chars()`, so no function can split a multi-byte character. `chars.as_str()` returns the not-yet-consumed rest of the string as a slice without copying.

`é` is 2 bytes in UTF-8; `len` counts bytes.

questions.q: Why is `s[0]` a compile error for a String?
options: A byte index may not be a whole character, and finding the n-th char is not instant
questions.explanation: Rust refuses to give a surprising answer or hide a slow scan.

questions.q: Which builds `"x=1, y=2"` from `let x = 1; let y = 2;` without moving anything?
questions.explanation: `format!` returns a new String and only borrows its arguments.
`í` is 2 bytes (bytes 1 and 2), so byte 2 is inside it and the slice panics.

points: `String` is owned, growable UTF-8; `&str` is a borrowed slice of UTF-8.
Grow with `push_str` and `push`; join with `+` (moves the left side) or `format!` (moves nothing).
UTF-8 characters take 1 to 4 bytes, so strings cannot be indexed by position, and `len()` counts bytes.
Choose `bytes()`, `chars()` or (with a crate) graphemes depending on what you mean by "character".
Byte-range slices must fall on char boundaries or they panic.

terms.def: A text encoding that stores each Unicode character in 1 to 4 bytes; Rust strings always hold valid UTF-8.
An owned, growable UTF-8 text buffer (a wrapper around Vec<u8>).
A macro like println! that returns the formatted String instead of printing it.
What a reader perceives as one letter; may be several chars. Not in the standard library.
